chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yahya ibn Uqba al-Azdi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: 'The example of the one greedy for the world is like the example of a silkworm. The more it wraps around itself, the further it gets from exiting, until it dies in sorrow.'

He said, and Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'Among what Luqman advised his son with was: O my son! The people before you had amassed for their children, but what they amassed did not remain, nor did they remain, the ones it was amassed for. Rather, you are a hired servant who has been ordered to do a work and promised a reward for it.'

So fulfill your work and fully receive your reward, and do not be in this world like a sheep that fell into a green crop, ate until it fattened, and its death was at the time of its fattening. But make the world like a bridge over a river; you cross it and leave it, and do not return to it for the rest of your life. Ruin it and do not build it up, for you have not been ordered to build it up.

And know that you will be asked tomorrow when you stand before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, about four things: your youth, regarding what you wore it down; your life, regarding what you spent it; your wealth, from what you earned it and on what you spent it. So prepare for that and prepare an answer for it, and do not grieve over what has passed from the world, for the little of the world does not remain, and its much is not safe from calamity.

So take your precaution and strive in your affair, and uncover the covering from your face, and expose yourself to the goodness of your Lord, and renew repentance in your heart, and withdraw during your leisure before your journey is undertaken, your decree is executed, and a barrier is placed between you and what you intend.
ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic perspective on worldly attachment and how should one prepare for the afterlife?
ai.summary: This hadith, narrated from Imam al-Baqir and Imam al-Sadiq, synthesizes Luqman’s wisdom with Imami teachings to critique material accumulation through the metaphor of the silkworm, whose self-wrapping leads to suffocation. It urges believers to treat the world as a transient bridge rather than a permanent residence, emphasizing accountability for youth, lifespan, wealth, and expenditure as highlighted in Shia exegetical traditions.
